title: Earth to the Moon
subtitle: The coast of Apollo 11
sourceNote: 384,400 km is the mean Earth-Moon distance; the orbit is elliptical, so the real figure varies by about 10%.

waypoints.name: Low Earth orbit
waypoints.body: Parking orbit, and where the Space Station still is today. Getting this far took most of the fuel — and it is under a twentieth of one percent of the trip.

waypoints.name: Translunar injection
waypoints.body: The third stage burns for six minutes and the spacecraft stops circling Earth and starts falling towards the Moon.

waypoints.name: Geostationary orbit
waypoints.body: Where television and weather satellites sit, matching Earth's spin so they hang over one spot. Nine percent of the way.

waypoints.name: The whole Earth in one frame
waypoints.body: Far enough that the planet fits in a window. Apollo 11 passed here about ten hours after leaving orbit.

waypoints.name: Halfway
waypoints.body: Still coasting, still slowing down — the ship is climbing out of Earth's gravity the whole way and is at its slowest near the end.

waypoints.name: The point of no return
waypoints.body: Ninety percent out, and the Moon's gravity now pulls harder than Earth's. From here you are falling towards the Moon, not away from home.

waypoints.name: The Moon
waypoints.body: Three days and about seventy-six hours after launch. Radio signals from here take one and a quarter seconds to reach Earth.
